writeup.1: In 1962 a golfer called Jan Craig, out on a rural route outside Cincinnati, made her own headcovers in worsted wool because she could not buy any she liked for a new set of clubs. Jack Nicklaus ordered a set within a few years, Tom Watson carried them, and so did multiple Ryder Cup teams. Every cover is still hand-knit to order, and the only design change in six decades was elastic inside the driver.
writeup.2: The animal headcover came seventeen years later, from a mother and daughter in Phoenix. Frank, the tiger, went on Tiger Woods’ driver at the 1997 Masters, Nike licensed the character and named him, and the business grew four hundred per cent in a quarter.
writeup.3: Neither of those is a novelty company, and neither is interesting only for who started it. Seventeen brands do both things at once: founded or co-founded by a woman, and making what men buy, which is headcovers, leather, bags, gloves, towels, socks, polos and shoes. Almost every women-founded golf brand makes women’s apparel and nothing else, and almost every independent brand making unisex hard goods was founded by men, so the overlap between the two runs thin.
writeup.4: One pattern turns up again and again. Megan Chisti co-founded Seamus, trained as the designer, rebuilt the headcover that started the company and still sews product, and there is no published quote from her anywhere. Gail Hanson co-founded Bluetross, and the first prototypes came off her inherited sewing machine; the biggest feature ever written about the company is headlined “the unlikely story of a man who quit his job to make leather headcovers.” Neither brand is hiding anything, and both credit her plainly on their own About page. The voice just defaults to him. So every entry names the woman, and says plainly when she co-founded with a husband or a mother rather than rounding up.
